4. **Noble Immunities** - Nobles could maintain personal armies, weren't obliged to serve the king, and had significant judicial independence.

5. **Political Autonomy of Estates** - Nobles controlled taxation, land policy, and local government decisions independently.

6. **Constitution of May 3, 1791** - After Russia invaded, they forced Poland to abandon this radical liberal constitution, restoring previous restrictive practices.

- Poland remained under occupation for 123 years until regaining independence in 1918
- Each empire governed its portion using its own imperial legal system, systematically abolishing Polish noble privileges and replacing them with authoritarian imperial control

|  The three partitions of Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth: the Russian Partition (brown), the Austrian Partition (green), and the Prussian Partition (blue) |
The **Partitions of Poland**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-1) were three partitions of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth that took place between 1772 and 1795, toward the end of the 18th century. The partitions ended the existence of the state, resulting in the elimination of sovereign Poland and Lithuania for 123 years. The partitions were conducted by the Habsburg monarchy, the Kingdom of Prussia, and the Russian Empire, which divided up the commonwealth's lands among themselves progressively in the process of territorial seizures and annexations.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Brit-2)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-3)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-4)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-5)

The First Partition was decided on 5 August 1772, after the Bar Confederation lost the war with Russia. The Second Partition occurred in the aftermath of the Polish–Russian War of 1792 and the Targowica Confederation, when Russian and Prussian troops entered the commonwealth and the partition treaty was signed during the Grodno Sejm on 23 January 1793 (without Austria). The Third Partition took place on 24 October 1795, in reaction to the unsuccessful Polish Kościuszko Uprising the previous year. With this partition, the commonwealth ceased to exist.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Brit-2)
In English, the term "Partitions of Poland" is sometimes used geographically as toponymy, to mean the three parts that the partitioning powers divided the commonwealth into, namely: the Austrian Partition, the Prussian Partition and the Russian Partition. In Polish, there are two separate words for the two meanings. The consecutive acts of dividing and annexation of Poland are referred to as _\_rozbiór\__ (plural: _\_rozbiory\__), while the term _\_zabór\__ (plural: _\_zabory\__) refers to parts of the commonwealth that were annexed in 1772–1795 and which became part of Imperial Russia, Prussia, or Austria. Following the Congress of Vienna in 1815, the borders of the three partitioned sectors were redrawn; the Austrians established Galicia in the Austrian partition, whereas the Russians gained Warsaw from Prussia and formed an autonomous polity known as Congress Poland in the Russian partition.
In Polish historiography, the term "Fourth Partition of Poland" has also been used, in reference to any subsequent annexation of Polish lands by foreign invaders. Depending on source and historical period, this could mean the events of 1815, or 1832 and 1846, or 1939.

The term "Fourth Partition" in a temporal sense can also mean the diaspora communities that played an important political role in re-establishing the Polish sovereign state after 1918: after the end of World War I, the Central Powers' surrender to the Western Allies, the chaos of the Russian Revolution and the Treaty of Versailles finally allowed for the restoration of Poland's full independence after 123 years.
Allegory of the first partition of Poland, showing Catherine the Great of Russia (left), Joseph II of Austria (middle) and Frederick the Great of Prussia (right) quarrelling over their territorial seizures
Włodzimierz Tetmajer, _Allegory of Dead Poland_, St. Nicholas Cathedral, Kalisz
During the reign of Władysław IV (1632–1648), the _liberum veto_ was developed, a policy of parliamentary procedure based on the assumption of the political equality of every "gentleman/Polish nobleman", with the corollary that unanimous consent was needed for all measures.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Brit-2) A single member of parliament's belief that a measure was injurious to his own constituency (usually simply his own estate), even after the act had been approved, became enough to strike the act. Thus, it became increasingly difficult to undertake action. The _liberum veto_ also provided openings for foreign diplomats to get their way, through bribing nobles to exercise it.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Brit-2) Thus, one could characterise Poland–Lithuania in its final period (mid-18th century) before the partitions as already in a state of disorder and not a completely sovereign state, and almost as a vassal state,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Scott-6) with Polish kings effectively chosen in diplomatic maneuvers between the great powers Prussia, Austria, Russia and France.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Corwin-7) This applies particularly to the last Commonwealth King Stanisław August Poniatowski, who for some time had been a lover of Russian Empress Catherine the Great.

In 1730, the neighbors of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth (_Rzeczpospolita_), namely Prussia, Austria and Russia, signed a secret agreement to maintain the _status quo_: specifically, to ensure that the commonwealth laws would not change. Their alliance later became known in Poland as the "Alliance of the Three Black Eagles" (or _\_Löwenwolde\_'s Treaty_), because all three states used a black eagle as a state symbol (in contrast to the white eagle, a symbol of Poland). The commonwealth had been forced to rely on Russia for protection against the rising Kingdom of Prussia, which demanded a slice of the northwest in order to unite its Western and Eastern portions; this would leave the commonwealth with a Baltic coast only in Latvia and Lithuania.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Brit-2) Catherine had to use diplomacy to win Austria to her side.

The commonwealth had remained neutral in the [Seven Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Years'_War "Seven Years' War") (1756–1763), yet it sympathised with the alliance of France, Austria, and Russia, and allowed Russian troops access to its western lands as bases against Prussia. Frederick II retaliated by ordering enough Polish currency counterfeited to severely affect the Polish economy. Through the Polish nobles whom Russia controlled and the Russian Minister to Warsaw, ambassador and Prince Nicholas Repnin, Empress Catherine the Great forced a constitution on the commonwealth at the so-called Repnin Sejm of 1767, named after ambassador Repnin, who effectively dictated the terms of that Sejm (and ordered the capture and exile to Kaluga of some vocal opponents of his policies,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Scott-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Steed,-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Seton-Watson-9) including bishop Józef Andrzej Załuski[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Cas-10) and others). This new constitution undid the reforms made in 1764 under Stanisław II. The _liberum veto_ and all the old abuses of the last one and a half centuries were guaranteed as unalterable parts of this new constitution (in the so-called _Cardinal Laws_[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Seton-Watson-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-RB-11)). Repnin also demanded the Russian protection of the rights of peasants in private estates of Polish and Lithuanian noblemen, religious freedom for the Protestant and Orthodox Christians and the political freedoms for Protestants, Orthodox Christians and Eastern Catholics (Uniates), including their right to occupy all state positions, including a royal one. The next king could be a member of the Russian ruling dynasty now. The Sejm approved this.

The Third Partition of Poland, finalized on October 24, 1795, marked the complete dissolution of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, which had once been a significant power in Europe. This partition involved the division of the last independent Polish territories among the three neighboring powers: Austria, Prussia, and Russia. The roots of Poland's decline can be traced back to a weak central authority, largely due to the fragmented interests of the Polish nobility, who prioritized their local power over national unity. Despite efforts by some Poles to resist foreign domination, many nobles chose to align with external forces, leading to earlier partitions in 1772 and 1793. The cumulative actions of these neighboring states, including bribing influential nobles, contributed to Poland's eventual loss of sovereignty. The final partition resulted in Russia absorbing about half of the remaining Polish lands, while Austria and Prussia each acquired approximately a quarter. Following this division, Poland would remain partitioned and under foreign control until it regained independence in the 20th century.

## Full article
### Third Partition of Poland
On October 24, 1795, the European powers of Austria, Prussia, and Russia agreed upon their third and final partition of the once mighty nation of Poland. The last independent Polish territories were split between them, and Poland would not reappear as an independent nation until the 20th century.
Poland had once been one of Europe's great powers. Polish kings had controlled much of western Russia and had been instrumental in defending Western Christendom by defeating the Ottoman Turks when their invading armies nearly reached the gates of Vienna in the late 17th century. However, central authority was weak, due to the self-serving actions of the Polish nobility, who jealously guarded their privileges, interests, and local power regardless of the welfare of the nation. Since kings had to be elected by the nobles, it was difficult to build any lasting national government able to resist the centrifugal forces at work. Poland's neighbors Austria, Prussia, and Russia furthered the process of disintegration by bribing or otherwise influencing important nobles to support their various interests or causes. By 1772 Poland was so weak that these neighboring powers simply decided to take various portions of the country for themselves, an agreement known as the First Partition of Poland which led to the distribution of roughly one-fourth of the land to the Austrians, Prussians, and Russians.
Although many Poles put their nation first and fought bravely to preserve its freedom, too many of the nobles were willing to ally themselves with foreign interests. This happened in 1792 when nobles who opposed a new constitution designed to strengthen Poland's central government asked Empress Catherine the Great of Russia for assistance. The result was a Russian invasion of Poland, in which Russia crushed its opponents. The conflict ended in 1793 with the Second Partition of Poland, which awarded even more of the country to its neighbors. In 1795, thanks in large part to continuing resistance from Polish loyalists, the Austrians, Prussians, and Russians decided to take all that remained of the nation in a third and final partition. This was largely completed by 1797. Russia received approximately half of the remaining lands, while Austria and Prussia each got roughly one-quarter of them.

On 25 November 1795, King Stanislaw II Augustus of Poland abdicated from his throne, and in the process the Commonwealth of Poland-Lithuania was wiped off the map of Europe. This was the Third of three partitions of Poland between Russia, Prussia, and Austria, which over the course of twenty years reduced a once mighty kingdom to nought. This post establishes the events of the partitions and examines the causes behind them.
Poland-Lithuania was one of the most powerful states in late medieval and early modern Europe. In 1410 King Wladyslaw Jagiello of Poland in alliance with his cousin Grand Duke Vytautas of Lithuania won a famous victory over the Teutonic Knights at the Battle of Grunwald. King Stepan Bathory of Poland successfully thwarted Russian Tsar Ivan the Terrible’s efforts to gain a foothold in Livonia in the 1570s. By the 1610s Polish troops occupied the Kremlin in Moscow and a Muscovite assembly had elected Crown Prince Wladyslaw as Tsar.
By the 17th century, however, the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth was already in decline. The Zaporizhian Cossack Bohdan Khmelnytsky’s uprising against Polish rule in 1654 ushered a series of unsuccessful campaigns known as The Deluge, when Russian and Swedish forces made significant gains against Poland over five years. Despite a brief hurrah during the reign of King Jan Sobieski, Poland’s fortunes failed to revive in the 18th century. In 1700 Poland entered the Great Northern War against Sweden as the senior partner alongside its Russian and Danish allies. By the time the war ended in 1721, it was clear that Russia had leapfrogged Poland as Eastern Europe’s leading power.
Royal Castle, palace square facade. Warsaw, Poland.

For much of the 18th century, Poland became effectively a Russian protectorate. In 1764, following the death of King Augustus III, Russian Empress Catherine II had her ex-lover Stanislaw August Poniatowski elected to the throne as King Stanislaw II. Catherine expected that the new Polish king would act as a Russian puppet. Stanislaw confounded expectations and pursued energetic reforms aimed at strengthening the Polish state. Ever since the extinction of the Jagiellonian Dynasty in 1572, Poland’s kings were elected by the Sejm (parliament). The constitution gave Polish noblemen a range of liberties and privileges that did not exist in other European kingdoms. Polish magnates could have their personal armies and were not obliged to serve the king.
The weak central authority in Poland allowed its neighbours – Austria, Russia, and Prussia – to champion various individuals and various factions. All three states were expanding their territories, and while Poland seemed like easy fruit, it also served as a useful buffer state between the three major powers. Thus, it was in everyone’s interest to maintain Poland as an independent state with a weak central authority.
The first challenge to Stanislaw’s reforms did not come from any of these states but from a group of Polish nobles who in 1768 formed the Bar Confederation at the fortress of Bar in modern day Ukraine. These influential nobles, supported by France, opposed both Stanislaw’s reforms and Russian influence in Poland. The Bar Confederation initiated a war with Russia which lasted four years and resulted in eventual Russian victory. As a result, Russia’s influence in central Europe increased.
King Stanislaw II Augustus Poniatowski. Royal Castle, Warsaw, Poland.
Russia’s victory against the Bar Confederation, as well as military success against the Ottoman Empire, caused the Austrian Habsburg Empire to feel uneasy. In order to prevent the outbreak of war, Frederick the Great proposed a partition of Poland between the three powers. This was intended to clip the wings of Poland’s independently-minded king as well as provide Austria with territorial compensation for Russia’s increased power. Although Empress Maria Theresia was reluctant to carve up Poland, she realised that it was the most pragmatic action for the security of her state. Frederick remarked of the Habsburg Empress during the negotiations between the three monarchs, ‘the more she wept, the more she took.’

The ensuing treaty was drawn up by the partitioning powers, which forced Stanislaw and his Sejm to ratify the document. Prussia received a piece of territory to the northwest with a population of 580,000. Although this was the smallest piece of the partition both in terms of territory and population, it proved of immense value to Prussia since the area was more economically developed than the others, and it also formed a crucial territorial link between Prussian territories in East Prussia and Brandenburg. Austria received a significant piece of territory to the south and increased its population by 2.5 million. Russia received the largest chunk of land to the east with 1.3 million men, but it was poorly developed. Nevertheless, this did provide Russia with a more secure western frontier and Poland was formally recognised as a Russian protectorate.
Over the ensuing two decades and despite the partition, King Stanislaw continued to pursue reforms to strengthen his authority but was hamstrung in the Sejm due to noble opposition. In 1788 a new Sejm was convened which offered the most radical reform. They worked on a new constitution, inspired by the writings of Rousseau and the English and American constitution, but one which also provided for greater authority of the state. King Stanislaw supported the reformers, who presented their Constitution on 3 May.
The Polish Constitution infuriated the Russian empress, who believed that the Poles were suffering from the ‘Jacobin madness.’ A group of conservative Polish noblemen were equally opposed to the constitution and formed the Confederation of Targowica to challenge the new Constitution. The confederation requested support from Russia which duly arrived. Although Stanislaw had been promised 100,000 men by the Sejm for his army, due to the short timeframe fewer than 40,000 could be summoned. Under the command of the king’s nephew Jozef Poniatowski (future Marshal of the French Empire) and Tadeusz Kosciusko, a veteran of the American Revolutionary War, Stanislaw’s army managed to win several heroic victories, but eventually the greater numbers of the Russians decided the matter.

By July 1792 the capital city of Warsaw was under siege and Stanislaw Augustus reckoned that the was no option but to surrender. Having received assurances from the Russian ambassador that no territorial changes would take place, Stanislaw joined the Targowica Confederation while the Polish pro-constitution army disintegrated. The Targowica confederates hoped that Russia would restore the previous Polish political system. Although Russia did indeed repeal the Constitution of 3 May, both the King and the Targowica confederates were dismayed to learn of another partition treaty between Russia and Prussia, Poland’s erstwhile ally. Prussia took the city of Poznan, the ports of Gdansk and Elbląg and the fortress of Torún, while the Russians gained large parts of modern day Belarus and Ukraine including Minsk.
Following the Second Partition of 1793, Poland’s population stood at a third of what it had been prior to the First Partition. The punitive settlement was not popular and did not endure for long. Both the King and the conservatives lost much prestige while the reformers gained popularity. In 1794 General Kosciusko launched an uprising against Prussia and Russia in an attempt to overturn the Second Partition. Although Stanislaw did not sanction the uprising, he considered it his patriotic duty to support Kosciusko’s efforts. Much like the previous war, Kosciusko’s armies showed immense courage on the battlefield and won several victories, but in the end were outnumbered and defeated by the Russians commanded by Alexander Suvorov.
General Tadeusz Kosciuszko announces his uprising in Krakow’s market square.
The failure of the Kosciusko Uprising was the death knell of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. Prussia and Russia were ready to wipe the country entirely off the map. Austria, once again a reluctant partner, decided that it was best to partake in the spoils rather than miss out as it had done so in 1793. Accordingly the remainder of Poland-Lithuania was divided between the three countries. The capital Warsaw and 1 million inhabitants went to Prussia. The Russians took the Lithuanian capital of Vilnius and a population of 1.2 million, while the Austrian share included the cities of Krakow and Lublin and 1.2 million people in total.

This map shows the three partitions of Poland in 1772, 1793, 1795 by Russia, Prussia, and Austria. The

On 25 November 1795, King Stanislaw II Augustus of Poland abdicated from his throne, and in the process the Commonwealth of Poland-Lithuania was wiped off the map of Europe. This was the Third of three partitions of Poland between Russia, Prussia, and Austria, which over the course of twenty years reduced a once mighty kingdom to nought. This post establishes the events of the partitions and examines the causes behind them.
Poland-Lithuania was one of the most powerful states in late medieval and early modern Europe. In 1410 King Wladyslaw Jagiello of Poland in alliance with his cousin Grand Duke Vytautas of Lithuania won a famous victory over the Teutonic Knights at the Battle of Grunwald. King Stepan Bathory of Poland successfully thwarted Russian Tsar Ivan the Terrible’s efforts to gain a foothold in Livonia in the 1570s. By the 1610s Polish troops occupied the Kremlin in Moscow and a Muscovite assembly had elected Crown Prince Wladyslaw as Tsar.
By the 17th century, however, the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth was already in decline. The Zaporizhian Cossack Bohdan Khmelnytsky’s uprising against Polish rule in 1654 ushered a series of unsuccessful campaigns known as The Deluge, when Russian and Swedish forces made significant gains against Poland over five years. Despite a brief hurrah during the reign of King Jan Sobieski, Poland’s fortunes failed to revive in the 18th century. In 1700 Poland entered the Great Northern War against Sweden as the senior partner alongside its Russian and Danish allies. By the time the war ended in 1721, it was clear that Russia had leapfrogged Poland as Eastern Europe’s leading power.
Royal Castle, palace square facade. Warsaw, Poland.
texts.1:
For much of the 18th century, Poland became effectively a Russian protectorate. In 1764, following the death of King Augustus III, Russian Empress Catherine II had her ex-lover Stanislaw August Poniatowski elected to the throne as King Stanislaw II. Catherine expected that the new Polish king would act as a Russian puppet. Stanislaw confounded expectations and pursued energetic reforms aimed at strengthening the Polish state. Ever since the extinction of the Jagiellonian Dynasty in 1572, Poland’s kings were elected by the Sejm (parliament). The constitution gave Polish noblemen a range of liberties and privileges that did not exist in other European kingdoms. Polish magnates could have their personal armies and were not obliged to serve the king.
The weak central authority in Poland allowed its neighbours – Austria, Russia, and Prussia – to champion various individuals and various factions. All three states were expanding their territories, and while Poland seemed like easy fruit, it also served as a useful buffer state between the three major powers. Thus, it was in everyone’s interest to maintain Poland as an independent state with a weak central authority.
The first challenge to Stanislaw’s reforms did not come from any of these states but from a group of Polish nobles who in 1768 formed the Bar Confederation at the fortress of Bar in modern day Ukraine. These influential nobles, supported by France, opposed both Stanislaw’s reforms and Russian influence in Poland. The Bar Confederation initiated a war with Russia which lasted four years and resulted in eventual Russian victory. As a result, Russia’s influence in central Europe increased.
King Stanislaw II Augustus Poniatowski. Royal Castle, Warsaw, Poland.
Russia’s victory against the Bar Confederation, as well as military success against the Ottoman Empire, caused the Austrian Habsburg Empire to feel uneasy. In order to prevent the outbreak of war, Frederick the Great proposed a partition of Poland between the three powers. This was intended to clip the wings of Poland’s independently-minded king as well as provide Austria with territorial compensation for Russia’s increased power. Although Empress Maria Theresia was reluctant to carve up Poland, she realised that it was the most pragmatic action for the security of her state. Frederick remarked of the Habsburg Empress during the negotiations between the three monarchs, ‘the more she wept, the more she took.’
texts.2:
The ensuing treaty was drawn up by the partitioning powers, which forced Stanislaw and his Sejm to ratify the document. Prussia received a piece of territory to the northwest with a population of 580,000. Although this was the smallest piece of the partition both in terms of territory and population, it proved of immense value to Prussia since the area was more economically developed than the others, and it also formed a crucial territorial link between Prussian territories in East Prussia and Brandenburg. Austria received a significant piece of territory to the south and increased its population by 2.5 million. Russia received the largest chunk of land to the east with 1.3 million men, but it was poorly developed. Nevertheless, this did provide Russia with a more secure western frontier and Poland was formally recognised as a Russian protectorate.
Over the ensuing two decades and despite the partition, King Stanislaw continued to pursue reforms to strengthen his authority but was hamstrung in the Sejm due to noble opposition. In 1788 a new Sejm was convened which offered the most radical reform. They worked on a new constitution, inspired by the writings of Rousseau and the English and American constitution, but one which also provided for greater authority of the state. King Stanislaw supported the reformers, who presented their Constitution on 3 May.
The Polish Constitution infuriated the Russian empress, who believed that the Poles were suffering from the ‘Jacobin madness.’ A group of conservative Polish noblemen were equally opposed to the constitution and formed the Confederation of Targowica to challenge the new Constitution. The confederation requested support from Russia which duly arrived. Although Stanislaw had been promised 100,000 men by the Sejm for his army, due to the short timeframe fewer than 40,000 could be summoned. Under the command of the king’s nephew Jozef Poniatowski (future Marshal of the French Empire) and Tadeusz Kosciusko, a veteran of the American Revolutionary War, Stanislaw’s army managed to win several heroic victories, but eventually the greater numbers of the Russians decided the matter.
texts.3:
By July 1792 the capital city of Warsaw was under siege and Stanislaw Augustus reckoned that the was no option but to surrender. Having received assurances from the Russian ambassador that no territorial changes would take place, Stanislaw joined the Targowica Confederation while the Polish pro-constitution army disintegrated. The Targowica confederates hoped that Russia would restore the previous Polish political system. Although Russia did indeed repeal the Constitution of 3 May, both the King and the Targowica confederates were dismayed to learn of another partition treaty between Russia and Prussia, Poland’s erstwhile ally. Prussia took the city of Poznan, the ports of Gdansk and Elbląg and the fortress of Torún, while the Russians gained large parts of modern day Belarus and Ukraine including Minsk.
Following the Second Partition of 1793, Poland’s population stood at a third of what it had been prior to the First Partition. The punitive settlement was not popular and did not endure for long. Both the King and the conservatives lost much prestige while the reformers gained popularity. In 1794 General Kosciusko launched an uprising against Prussia and Russia in an attempt to overturn the Second Partition. Although Stanislaw did not sanction the uprising, he considered it his patriotic duty to support Kosciusko’s efforts. Much like the previous war, Kosciusko’s armies showed immense courage on the battlefield and won several victories, but in the end were outnumbered and defeated by the Russians commanded by Alexander Suvorov.
General Tadeusz Kosciuszko announces his uprising in Krakow’s market square.
The failure of the Kosciusko Uprising was the death knell of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. Prussia and Russia were ready to wipe the country entirely off the map. Austria, once again a reluctant partner, decided that it was best to partake in the spoils rather than miss out as it had done so in 1793. Accordingly the remainder of Poland-Lithuania was divided between the three countries. The capital Warsaw and 1 million inhabitants went to Prussia. The Russians took the Lithuanian capital of Vilnius and a population of 1.2 million, while the Austrian share included the cities of Krakow and Lublin and 1.2 million people in total.

The Third Partition of Poland, finalized on October 24, 1795, marked the complete dissolution of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, which had once been a significant power in Europe. This partition involved the division of the last independent Polish territories among the three neighboring powers: Austria, Prussia, and Russia. The roots of Poland's decline can be traced back to a weak central authority, largely due to the fragmented interests of the Polish nobility, who prioritized their local power over national unity. Despite efforts by some Poles to resist foreign domination, many nobles chose to align with external forces, leading to earlier partitions in 1772 and 1793. The cumulative actions of these neighboring states, including bribing influential nobles, contributed to Poland's eventual loss of sovereignty. The final partition resulted in Russia absorbing about half of the remaining Polish lands, while Austria and Prussia each acquired approximately a quarter. Following this division, Poland would remain partitioned and under foreign control until it regained independence in the 20th century.

### Third Partition of Poland
On October 24, 1795, the European powers of Austria, Prussia, and Russia agreed upon their third and final partition of the once mighty nation of Poland. The last independent Polish territories were split between them, and Poland would not reappear as an independent nation until the 20th century.
Poland had once been one of Europe's great powers. Polish kings had controlled much of western Russia and had been instrumental in defending Western Christendom by defeating the Ottoman Turks when their invading armies nearly reached the gates of Vienna in the late 17th century. However, central authority was weak, due to the self-serving actions of the Polish nobility, who jealously guarded their privileges, interests, and local power regardless of the welfare of the nation. Since kings had to be elected by the nobles, it was difficult to build any lasting national government able to resist the centrifugal forces at work. Poland's neighbors Austria, Prussia, and Russia furthered the process of disintegration by bribing or otherwise influencing important nobles to support their various interests or causes. By 1772 Poland was so weak that these neighboring powers simply decided to take various portions of the country for themselves, an agreement known as the First Partition of Poland which led to the distribution of roughly one-fourth of the land to the Austrians, Prussians, and Russians.
Although many Poles put their nation first and fought bravely to preserve its freedom, too many of the nobles were willing to ally themselves with foreign interests. This happened in 1792 when nobles who opposed a new constitution designed to strengthen Poland's central government asked Empress Catherine the Great of Russia for assistance. The result was a Russian invasion of Poland, in which Russia crushed its opponents. The conflict ended in 1793 with the Second Partition of Poland, which awarded even more of the country to its neighbors. In 1795, thanks in large part to continuing resistance from Polish loyalists, the Austrians, Prussians, and Russians decided to take all that remained of the nation in a third and final partition. This was largely completed by 1797. Russia received approximately half of the remaining lands, while Austria and Prussia each got roughly one-quarter of them.

The **Partitions of Poland**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-1) were three partitions of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth that took place between 1772 and 1795, toward the end of the 18th century. The partitions ended the existence of the state, resulting in the elimination of sovereign Poland and Lithuania for 123 years. The partitions were conducted by the Habsburg monarchy, the Kingdom of Prussia, and the Russian Empire, which divided up the commonwealth's lands among themselves progressively in the process of territorial seizures and annexations.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Brit-2)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-3)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-4)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-5)
texts.1:
The First Partition was decided on 5 August 1772, after the Bar Confederation lost the war with Russia. The Second Partition occurred in the aftermath of the Polish–Russian War of 1792 and the Targowica Confederation, when Russian and Prussian troops entered the commonwealth and the partition treaty was signed during the Grodno Sejm on 23 January 1793 (without Austria). The Third Partition took place on 24 October 1795, in reaction to the unsuccessful Polish Kościuszko Uprising the previous year. With this partition, the commonwealth ceased to exist.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Brit-2)
In English, the term "Partitions of Poland" is sometimes used geographically as toponymy, to mean the three parts that the partitioning powers divided the commonwealth into, namely: the Austrian Partition, the Prussian Partition and the Russian Partition. In Polish, there are two separate words for the two meanings. The consecutive acts of dividing and annexation of Poland are referred to as _\_rozbiór\__ (plural: _\_rozbiory\__), while the term _\_zabór\__ (plural: _\_zabory\__) refers to parts of the commonwealth that were annexed in 1772–1795 and which became part of Imperial Russia, Prussia, or Austria. Following the Congress of Vienna in 1815, the borders of the three partitioned sectors were redrawn; the Austrians established Galicia in the Austrian partition, whereas the Russians gained Warsaw from Prussia and formed an autonomous polity known as Congress Poland in the Russian partition.
In Polish historiography, the term "Fourth Partition of Poland" has also been used, in reference to any subsequent annexation of Polish lands by foreign invaders. Depending on source and historical period, this could mean the events of 1815, or 1832 and 1846, or 1939.
texts.2:
The term "Fourth Partition" in a temporal sense can also mean the diaspora communities that played an important political role in re-establishing the Polish sovereign state after 1918: after the end of World War I, the Central Powers' surrender to the Western Allies, the chaos of the Russian Revolution and the Treaty of Versailles finally allowed for the restoration of Poland's full independence after 123 years.
Allegory of the first partition of Poland, showing Catherine the Great of Russia (left), Joseph II of Austria (middle) and Frederick the Great of Prussia (right) quarrelling over their territorial seizures
Włodzimierz Tetmajer, _Allegory of Dead Poland_, St. Nicholas Cathedral, Kalisz
During the reign of Władysław IV (1632–1648), the _liberum veto_ was developed, a policy of parliamentary procedure based on the assumption of the political equality of every "gentleman/Polish nobleman", with the corollary that unanimous consent was needed for all measures.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Brit-2) A single member of parliament's belief that a measure was injurious to his own constituency (usually simply his own estate), even after the act had been approved, became enough to strike the act. Thus, it became increasingly difficult to undertake action. The _liberum veto_ also provided openings for foreign diplomats to get their way, through bribing nobles to exercise it.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Brit-2) Thus, one could characterise Poland–Lithuania in its final period (mid-18th century) before the partitions as already in a state of disorder and not a completely sovereign state, and almost as a vassal state,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Scott-6) with Polish kings effectively chosen in diplomatic maneuvers between the great powers Prussia, Austria, Russia and France.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Corwin-7) This applies particularly to the last Commonwealth King Stanisław August Poniatowski, who for some time had been a lover of Russian Empress Catherine the Great.
texts.3: In 1730, the neighbors of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth (_Rzeczpospolita_), namely Prussia, Austria and Russia, signed a secret agreement to maintain the _status quo_: specifically, to ensure that the commonwealth laws would not change. Their alliance later became known in Poland as the "Alliance of the Three Black Eagles" (or _\_Löwenwolde\_'s Treaty_), because all three states used a black eagle as a state symbol (in contrast to the white eagle, a symbol of Poland). The commonwealth had been forced to rely on Russia for protection against the rising Kingdom of Prussia, which demanded a slice of the northwest in order to unite its Western and Eastern portions; this would leave the commonwealth with a Baltic coast only in Latvia and Lithuania.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Brit-2) Catherine had to use diplomacy to win Austria to her side.
texts.4: The commonwealth had remained neutral in the [Seven Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Years'_War "Seven Years' War") (1756–1763), yet it sympathised with the alliance of France, Austria, and Russia, and allowed Russian troops access to its western lands as bases against Prussia. Frederick II retaliated by ordering enough Polish currency counterfeited to severely affect the Polish economy. Through the Polish nobles whom Russia controlled and the Russian Minister to Warsaw, ambassador and Prince Nicholas Repnin, Empress Catherine the Great forced a constitution on the commonwealth at the so-called Repnin Sejm of 1767, named after ambassador Repnin, who effectively dictated the terms of that Sejm (and ordered the capture and exile to Kaluga of some vocal opponents of his policies,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Scott-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Steed,-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Seton-Watson-9) including bishop Józef Andrzej Załuski[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Cas-10) and others). This new constitution undid the reforms made in 1764 under Stanisław II. The _liberum veto_ and all the old abuses of the last one and a half centuries were guaranteed as unalterable parts of this new constitution (in the so-called _Cardinal Laws_[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Seton-Watson-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-RB-11)). Repnin also demanded the Russian protection of the rights of peasants in private estates of Polish and Lithuanian noblemen, religious freedom for the Protestant and Orthodox Christians and the political freedoms for Protestants, Orthodox Christians and Eastern Catholics (Uniates), including their right to occupy all state positions, including a royal one. The next king could be a member of the Russian ruling dynasty now. The Sejm approved this.

Abstract
This map shows the three partitions of Poland in 1772, 1793, 1795 by Russia, Prussia, and Austria. The

On 25 November 1795, King Stanislaw II Augustus of Poland abdicated from his throne, and in the process the Commonwealth of Poland-Lithuania was wiped off the map of Europe. This was the Third of three partitions of Poland between Russia, Prussia, and Austria, which over the course of twenty years reduced a once mighty kingdom to nought. This post establishes the events of the partitions and examines the causes behind them.
Poland-Lithuania was one of the most powerful states in late medieval and early modern Europe. In 1410 King Wladyslaw Jagiello of Poland in alliance with his cousin Grand Duke Vytautas of Lithuania won a famous victory over the Teutonic Knights at the Battle of Grunwald. King Stepan Bathory of Poland successfully thwarted Russian Tsar Ivan the Terrible’s efforts to gain a foothold in Livonia in the 1570s. By the 1610s Polish troops occupied the Kremlin in Moscow and a Muscovite assembly had elected Crown Prince Wladyslaw as Tsar.
By the 17th century, however, the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth was already in decline. The Zaporizhian Cossack Bohdan Khmelnytsky’s uprising against Polish rule in 1654 ushered a series of unsuccessful campaigns known as The Deluge, when Russian and Swedish forces made significant gains against Poland over five years. Despite a brief hurrah during the reign of King Jan Sobieski, Poland’s fortunes failed to revive in the 18th century. In 1700 Poland entered the Great Northern War against Sweden as the senior partner alongside its Russian and Danish allies. By the time the war ended in 1721, it was clear that Russia had leapfrogged Poland as Eastern Europe’s leading power.
Royal Castle, palace square facade. Warsaw, Poland.

For much of the 18th century, Poland became effectively a Russian protectorate. In 1764, following the death of King Augustus III, Russian Empress Catherine II had her ex-lover Stanislaw August Poniatowski elected to the throne as King Stanislaw II. Catherine expected that the new Polish king would act as a Russian puppet. Stanislaw confounded expectations and pursued energetic reforms aimed at strengthening the Polish state. Ever since the extinction of the Jagiellonian Dynasty in 1572, Poland’s kings were elected by the Sejm (parliament). The constitution gave Polish noblemen a range of liberties and privileges that did not exist in other European kingdoms. Polish magnates could have their personal armies and were not obliged to serve the king.
The weak central authority in Poland allowed its neighbours – Austria, Russia, and Prussia – to champion various individuals and various factions. All three states were expanding their territories, and while Poland seemed like easy fruit, it also served as a useful buffer state between the three major powers. Thus, it was in everyone’s interest to maintain Poland as an independent state with a weak central authority.
The first challenge to Stanislaw’s reforms did not come from any of these states but from a group of Polish nobles who in 1768 formed the Bar Confederation at the fortress of Bar in modern day Ukraine. These influential nobles, supported by France, opposed both Stanislaw’s reforms and Russian influence in Poland. The Bar Confederation initiated a war with Russia which lasted four years and resulted in eventual Russian victory. As a result, Russia’s influence in central Europe increased.
King Stanislaw II Augustus Poniatowski. Royal Castle, Warsaw, Poland.
Russia’s victory against the Bar Confederation, as well as military success against the Ottoman Empire, caused the Austrian Habsburg Empire to feel uneasy. In order to prevent the outbreak of war, Frederick the Great proposed a partition of Poland between the three powers. This was intended to clip the wings of Poland’s independently-minded king as well as provide Austria with territorial compensation for Russia’s increased power. Although Empress Maria Theresia was reluctant to carve up Poland, she realised that it was the most pragmatic action for the security of her state. Frederick remarked of the Habsburg Empress during the negotiations between the three monarchs, ‘the more she wept, the more she took.’

The ensuing treaty was drawn up by the partitioning powers, which forced Stanislaw and his Sejm to ratify the document. Prussia received a piece of territory to the northwest with a population of 580,000. Although this was the smallest piece of the partition both in terms of territory and population, it proved of immense value to Prussia since the area was more economically developed than the others, and it also formed a crucial territorial link between Prussian territories in East Prussia and Brandenburg. Austria received a significant piece of territory to the south and increased its population by 2.5 million. Russia received the largest chunk of land to the east with 1.3 million men, but it was poorly developed. Nevertheless, this did provide Russia with a more secure western frontier and Poland was formally recognised as a Russian protectorate.
Over the ensuing two decades and despite the partition, King Stanislaw continued to pursue reforms to strengthen his authority but was hamstrung in the Sejm due to noble opposition. In 1788 a new Sejm was convened which offered the most radical reform. They worked on a new constitution, inspired by the writings of Rousseau and the English and American constitution, but one which also provided for greater authority of the state. King Stanislaw supported the reformers, who presented their Constitution on 3 May.
The Polish Constitution infuriated the Russian empress, who believed that the Poles were suffering from the ‘Jacobin madness.’ A group of conservative Polish noblemen were equally opposed to the constitution and formed the Confederation of Targowica to challenge the new Constitution. The confederation requested support from Russia which duly arrived. Although Stanislaw had been promised 100,000 men by the Sejm for his army, due to the short timeframe fewer than 40,000 could be summoned. Under the command of the king’s nephew Jozef Poniatowski (future Marshal of the French Empire) and Tadeusz Kosciusko, a veteran of the American Revolutionary War, Stanislaw’s army managed to win several heroic victories, but eventually the greater numbers of the Russians decided the matter.

By July 1792 the capital city of Warsaw was under siege and Stanislaw Augustus reckoned that the was no option but to surrender. Having received assurances from the Russian ambassador that no territorial changes would take place, Stanislaw joined the Targowica Confederation while the Polish pro-constitution army disintegrated. The Targowica confederates hoped that Russia would restore the previous Polish political system. Although Russia did indeed repeal the Constitution of 3 May, both the King and the Targowica confederates were dismayed to learn of another partition treaty between Russia and Prussia, Poland’s erstwhile ally. Prussia took the city of Poznan, the ports of Gdansk and Elbląg and the fortress of Torún, while the Russians gained large parts of modern day Belarus and Ukraine including Minsk.
Following the Second Partition of 1793, Poland’s population stood at a third of what it had been prior to the First Partition. The punitive settlement was not popular and did not endure for long. Both the King and the conservatives lost much prestige while the reformers gained popularity. In 1794 General Kosciusko launched an uprising against Prussia and Russia in an attempt to overturn the Second Partition. Although Stanislaw did not sanction the uprising, he considered it his patriotic duty to support Kosciusko’s efforts. Much like the previous war, Kosciusko’s armies showed immense courage on the battlefield and won several victories, but in the end were outnumbered and defeated by the Russians commanded by Alexander Suvorov.
General Tadeusz Kosciuszko announces his uprising in Krakow’s market square.
The failure of the Kosciusko Uprising was the death knell of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. Prussia and Russia were ready to wipe the country entirely off the map. Austria, once again a reluctant partner, decided that it was best to partake in the spoils rather than miss out as it had done so in 1793. Accordingly the remainder of Poland-Lithuania was divided between the three countries. The capital Warsaw and 1 million inhabitants went to Prussia. The Russians took the Lithuanian capital of Vilnius and a population of 1.2 million, while the Austrian share included the cities of Krakow and Lublin and 1.2 million people in total.

### Third Partition of Poland
On October 24, 1795, the European powers of Austria, Prussia, and Russia agreed upon their third and final partition of the once mighty nation of Poland. The last independent Polish territories were split between them, and Poland would not reappear as an independent nation until the 20th century.
Poland had once been one of Europe's great powers. Polish kings had controlled much of western Russia and had been instrumental in defending Western Christendom by defeating the Ottoman Turks when their invading armies nearly reached the gates of Vienna in the late 17th century. However, central authority was weak, due to the self-serving actions of the Polish nobility, who jealously guarded their privileges, interests, and local power regardless of the welfare of the nation. Since kings had to be elected by the nobles, it was difficult to build any lasting national government able to resist the centrifugal forces at work. Poland's neighbors Austria, Prussia, and Russia furthered the process of disintegration by bribing or otherwise influencing important nobles to support their various interests or causes. By 1772 Poland was so weak that these neighboring powers simply decided to take various portions of the country for themselves, an agreement known as the First Partition of Poland which led to the distribution of roughly one-fourth of the land to the Austrians, Prussians, and Russians.
Although many Poles put their nation first and fought bravely to preserve its freedom, too many of the nobles were willing to ally themselves with foreign interests. This happened in 1792 when nobles who opposed a new constitution designed to strengthen Poland's central government asked Empress Catherine the Great of Russia for assistance. The result was a Russian invasion of Poland, in which Russia crushed its opponents. The conflict ended in 1793 with the Second Partition of Poland, which awarded even more of the country to its neighbors. In 1795, thanks in large part to continuing resistance from Polish loyalists, the Austrians, Prussians, and Russians decided to take all that remained of the nation in a third and final partition. This was largely completed by 1797. Russia received approximately half of the remaining lands, while Austria and Prussia each got roughly one-quarter of them.

The **Partitions of Poland**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-1) were three partitions of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth that took place between 1772 and 1795, toward the end of the 18th century. The partitions ended the existence of the state, resulting in the elimination of sovereign Poland and Lithuania for 123 years. The partitions were conducted by the Habsburg monarchy, the Kingdom of Prussia, and the Russian Empire, which divided up the commonwealth's lands among themselves progressively in the process of territorial seizures and annexations.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Brit-2)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-3)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-4)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-5)

The First Partition was decided on 5 August 1772, after the Bar Confederation lost the war with Russia. The Second Partition occurred in the aftermath of the Polish–Russian War of 1792 and the Targowica Confederation, when Russian and Prussian troops entered the commonwealth and the partition treaty was signed during the Grodno Sejm on 23 January 1793 (without Austria). The Third Partition took place on 24 October 1795, in reaction to the unsuccessful Polish Kościuszko Uprising the previous year. With this partition, the commonwealth ceased to exist.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Brit-2)
In English, the term "Partitions of Poland" is sometimes used geographically as toponymy, to mean the three parts that the partitioning powers divided the commonwealth into, namely: the Austrian Partition, the Prussian Partition and the Russian Partition. In Polish, there are two separate words for the two meanings. The consecutive acts of dividing and annexation of Poland are referred to as _\_rozbiór\__ (plural: _\_rozbiory\__), while the term _\_zabór\__ (plural: _\_zabory\__) refers to parts of the commonwealth that were annexed in 1772–1795 and which became part of Imperial Russia, Prussia, or Austria. Following the Congress of Vienna in 1815, the borders of the three partitioned sectors were redrawn; the Austrians established Galicia in the Austrian partition, whereas the Russians gained Warsaw from Prussia and formed an autonomous polity known as Congress Poland in the Russian partition.
In Polish historiography, the term "Fourth Partition of Poland" has also been used, in reference to any subsequent annexation of Polish lands by foreign invaders. Depending on source and historical period, this could mean the events of 1815, or 1832 and 1846, or 1939.

The term "Fourth Partition" in a temporal sense can also mean the diaspora communities that played an important political role in re-establishing the Polish sovereign state after 1918: after the end of World War I, the Central Powers' surrender to the Western Allies, the chaos of the Russian Revolution and the Treaty of Versailles finally allowed for the restoration of Poland's full independence after 123 years.

During the reign of Władysław IV (1632–1648), the _liberum veto_ was developed, a policy of parliamentary procedure based on the assumption of the political equality of every "gentleman/Polish nobleman", with the corollary that unanimous consent was needed for all measures.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Brit-2) A single member of parliament's belief that a measure was injurious to his own constituency (usually simply his own estate), even after the act had been approved, became enough to strike the act. Thus, it became increasingly difficult to undertake action. The _liberum veto_ also provided openings for foreign diplomats to get their way, through bribing nobles to exercise it.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Brit-2) Thus, one could characterise Poland–Lithuania in its final period (mid-18th century) before the partitions as already in a state of disorder and not a completely sovereign state, and almost as a vassal state,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Scott-6) with Polish kings effectively chosen in diplomatic maneuvers between the great powers Prussia, Austria, Russia and France.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Corwin-7) This applies particularly to the last Commonwealth King Stanisław August Poniatowski, who for some time had been a lover of Russian Empress Catherine the Great.

In 1730, the neighbors of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth (_Rzeczpospolita_), namely Prussia, Austria and Russia, signed a secret agreement to maintain the _status quo_: specifically, to ensure that the commonwealth laws would not change. Their alliance later became known in Poland as the "Alliance of the Three Black Eagles" (or _\_Löwenwolde\_'s Treaty_), because all three states used a black eagle as a state symbol (in contrast to the white eagle, a symbol of Poland). The commonwealth had been forced to rely on Russia for protection against the rising Kingdom of Prussia, which demanded a slice of the northwest in order to unite its Western and Eastern portions; this would leave the commonwealth with a Baltic coast only in Latvia and Lithuania.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Brit-2) Catherine had to use diplomacy to win Austria to her side.

The commonwealth had remained neutral in the [Seven Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Years'_War "Seven Years' War") (1756–1763), yet it sympathised with the alliance of France, Austria, and Russia, and allowed Russian troops access to its western lands as bases against Prussia. Frederick II retaliated by ordering enough Polish currency counterfeited to severely affect the Polish economy. Through the Polish nobles whom Russia controlled and the Russian Minister to Warsaw, ambassador and Prince Nicholas Repnin, Empress Catherine the Great forced a constitution on the commonwealth at the so-called Repnin Sejm of 1767, named after ambassador Repnin, who effectively dictated the terms of that Sejm (and ordered the capture and exile to Kaluga of some vocal opponents of his policies,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Scott-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Steed,-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Seton-Watson-9) including bishop Józef Andrzej Załuski[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Cas-10) and others). This new constitution undid the reforms made in 1764 under Stanisław II. The _liberum veto_ and all the old abuses of the last one and a half centuries were guaranteed as unalterable parts of this new constitution (in the so-called _Cardinal Laws_[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-Seton-Watson-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland#cite_note-RB-11)). Repnin also demanded the Russian protection of the rights of peasants in private estates of Polish and Lithuanian noblemen, religious freedom for the Protestant and Orthodox Christians and the political freedoms for Protestants, Orthodox Christians and Eastern Catholics (Uniates), including their right to occupy all state positions, including a royal one. The next king could be a member of the Russian ruling dynasty now. The Sejm approved this.
